stem: Let $P_n$ denote the real polynomials of degree at most $n$. What is $\dim P_n$?
correct: It is $n+1$, because the monomials $1,x,\dots,x^n$ form a basis of $P_n$ over the reals.
It is $n+1$, counting the monomials $1,\dots,x^n$.

distractors.text: It is $n$, because the constant polynomial $1$ is not counted.
It is infinite, because every coefficient ranges over a continuum.
distractors.misconception: confuses the size of the set with its dimension

distractors.text: It is $n!$, because the coefficients can be listed in $n!$ orders.
distractors.misconception: confuses orderings of coefficients with dimension

distractors.text: It is $n+2$, because the zero polynomial is one more basis vector.
distractors.misconception: counts the zero vector as a basis element

distractors.text: It is $2n$, because each power needs a positive and a negative coefficient.

explanation: The monomials $1,x,\dots,x^n$ span $P_n$ and are linearly independent, so there are $n+1$ basis vectors.

stem: Which of these subsets of the space $C[0,1]$ of continuous real functions on $[0,1]$ is a subspace?
correct: The set of all continuous $f$ with $f(0)=0$.
The functions vanishing at the endpoint $0$, as evaluation at $0$ is linear.

distractors.text: The set of all $f$ with $f(0)=1$, which is closed under taking averages.
distractors.misconception: overlooks that the zero function is missing

distractors.text: The set of all $f$ with $f(x)\ge 0$ for every $x$, a natural family of functions.
The set of all $f$ with $f(0)f(1)=0$, a product condition on two values.
The set of all $f$ with $|f(x)|\le 1$ for every $x$, a bounded family.
The set of all $f$ with $\int_0^1 f(x)^2\,dx=1$, a normalised family.
distractors.misconception: fails to contain the zero function and is not closed

explanation: A subspace needs the zero vector and closure under sums and scalar multiples. Only $f(0)=0$ is the kernel of the linear map $f\mapsto f(0)$.

stem: Consider the functions $1,\ \cos^2x,\ \sin^2x$ in the space $C(\mathbb{R})$. Which statement is true?
correct: They are linearly dependent, because $\cos^2x+\sin^2x-1=0$ holds for every real number $x$.
They are dependent, since $1=\cos^2x+\sin^2x$ holds for all real $x$.

distractors.text: They are linearly independent, because no one of them is a scalar multiple of another.
They are linearly independent, because the three graphs cross each other at several points.
They are dependent only on the interval $[0,\pi]$ and independent on all of $\mathbb{R}$.
distractors.misconception: thinks dependence can hold on part of the domain only

distractors.text: They are dependent, because $C(\mathbb{R})$ has finite dimension and three vectors are too many.
distractors.misconception: believes function spaces are finite dimensional

distractors.text: They are dependent, because all three take values in the interval $[0,1]$.
distractors.misconception: confuses a common range with linear dependence

explanation: Dependence means a nontrivial combination equals the zero function. The identity $\cos^2+\sin^2=1$ is such a combination. Pairwise non-proportionality is not enough.

stem: Let $V$ have dimension $n$. Which statement is true?
correct: Any $n$ linearly independent vectors in $V$ form a basis of the space $V$.
An independent list of length $n$ spans $V$.

distractors.text: Any $n$ vectors in $V$ span $V$, whether or not they are independent.
distractors.misconception: ignores that repeated vectors cannot span

distractors.text: Every spanning set of $V$ contains exactly $n$ vectors.
Any $n+1$ vectors in $V$ form a basis of $V$ as long as none is zero.
distractors.misconception: ignores that more than $n$ vectors are dependent

distractors.text: The dimension of $V$ changes when one passes to a different basis.
distractors.misconception: thinks dimension depends on the basis

distractors.text: Every basis of $V$ must contain a given nonzero vector $v$.
distractors.misconception: confuses extension to a basis with a forced element

explanation: In dimension $n$, independent lists have length at most $n$, and an independent list of length $n$ is a maximal one, hence a basis.

stem: Let $B=(b_1,\dots,b_n)$ be an ordered basis of $V$. The coordinate map $v\mapsto[v]_B\in\mathbb{R}^n$ is which kind of map?
correct: A linear bijection, so independent sets in $V$ match independent sets in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
An isomorphism from $V$ onto $\mathbb{R}^n$, preserving structure.

distractors.text: A linear map that is generally not injective, as many vectors share coordinates.
distractors.misconception: forgets that coordinates determine the vector

distractors.text: A map that is not linear, since coordinates change when the basis changes.
distractors.misconception: confuses dependence on the basis with nonlinearity

distractors.text: A map that is defined only when $B$ is an orthonormal basis of $V$.
distractors.misconception: thinks coordinates need an inner product

distractors.text: A map that sends each vector to its length with respect to the basis $B$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the coordinate vector with a norm

distractors.text: A map that does not depend on the order of the vectors in $B$.
distractors.misconception: forgets that reordering permutes the coordinates

explanation: Every $v$ is a unique combination $\sum c_ib_i$, and $[v]_B=(c_1,\dots,c_n)$. The map is linear, one-to-one and onto, but it depends on the order and choice of $B$.

stem: Let $T:V\to W$ be linear with $V$ finite dimensional. Which identity always holds?
correct: $\dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T=\dim V$, the dimension of the domain space.
Nullity plus rank equals $\dim V$.

distractors.text: $\dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T=\dim W$, the dimension of the codomain.
distractors.misconception: uses the codomain instead of the domain

distractors.text: $\dim\ker T=\dim\operatorname{im}T$, since the two subspaces correspond.
distractors.misconception: believes kernel and image are equally large

distractors.text: $\dim\operatorname{im}T=\dim V$ whenever the kernel is a proper subspace.
distractors.misconception: ignores that the image shrinks by the kernel dimension

distractors.text: $\dim\ker T\cdot\dim\operatorname{im}T=\dim V$, since kernel and image combine.
$\dim\ker T+\dim\operatorname{im}T=\dim V+\dim W$, counting both spaces.

explanation: This is the rank-nullity theorem. The kernel is what $T$ collapses and the image is what remains, so the two dimensions add to $\dim V$.

stem: Let $T:V\to V$ be a linear operator on a finite dimensional space. Which statement is correct?
correct: If $T$ is injective, then $T$ is also surjective, and so $\operatorname{im}T=V$ holds.
$\ker T=\{0\}$ forces $\operatorname{im}T=V$ for such operators.

distractors.text: An operator can be surjective and still have a nonzero kernel.
distractors.misconception: ignores rank-nullity for operators on one space

distractors.text: Injective operators are surjective only when $V$ is infinite dimensional.
distractors.misconception: reverses the finite and infinite cases

distractors.text: $T$ is injective exactly when $0$ does not lie in the image of $T$.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the zero vector is always in the image

distractors.text: The kernel of $T$ is nonzero exactly when the image of $T$ is nonzero.
For operators on a finite dimensional space, injectivity and surjectivity are independent properties.
distractors.misconception: true only for maps between spaces of different dimension

explanation: By rank-nullity, $\dim\operatorname{im}T=\dim V-\dim\ker T=\dim V$ when the kernel is zero, so the image is all of $V$. This fails in infinite dimensions, for example for the shift on sequences.

stem: The columns of the invertible matrix $P$ are the coordinates of the new basis $B'$ with respect to the old basis $B$. If $A=[T]_B$, what is $[T]_{B'}$?
correct: The matrix $P^{-1}AP$, a matrix similar to $A$ in the new basis.
$P^{-1}AP$ with the inverse on the left.

distractors.text: The matrix $PAP^{-1}$, with the factors in the other order.
distractors.misconception: swaps the roles of the two bases

distractors.text: The matrix $P^{\top}AP$, a congruence of $A$ by $P$.
The matrix $PAP$, using $P$ on both sides.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the inverse is needed

distractors.text: The matrix $A^{-1}PA$, conjugating $P$ by $A$.
distractors.misconception: mixes up which matrix is being conjugated

distractors.text: The matrix $PA$, since only the input coordinates change.
distractors.misconception: forgets that output coordinates change too

explanation: A vector with new coordinates $y$ has old coordinates $Py$. So $T$ in new coordinates is: convert to old coordinates, apply $A$, convert back, which is $P^{-1}AP$.

stem: Let $B=P^{-1}AP$ for an invertible $P$. Which property is shared by $A$ and $B$?
correct: They share the characteristic polynomial and hence all eigenvalues.
The same characteristic polynomial, so equal eigenvalues.

distractors.text: They have exactly the same eigenvectors, as column vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
distractors.misconception: forgets that eigenvectors are transformed by $P$

distractors.text: They have the same entries on the diagonal, since $P$ only moves entries around.
distractors.misconception: treats similarity as a permutation of entries

distractors.text: They are symmetric together, so a symmetric $A$ gives a symmetric $B$.
distractors.misconception: forgets that symmetry is not preserved by similarity

distractors.text: They have the same null space as subsets of $\mathbb{R}^n$.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the null space is mapped by $P^{-1}$

distractors.text: They have the same row space as subspaces of $\mathbb{R}^n$.

explanation: $\det(B-\lambda I)=\det(P^{-1}(A-\lambda I)P)=\det(A-\lambda I)$. Eigenvectors become $P^{-1}v$, and entries, symmetry and subspaces are not preserved.

stem: Two $n\times n$ matrices have the same characteristic polynomial. Which statement is correct?
correct: They need not be similar: $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ and the zero matrix share one.
The same characteristic polynomial is not sufficient.

distractors.text: They are similar, because the characteristic polynomial determines the matrix up to a change of basis.
distractors.misconception: treats the polynomial as a complete invariant

distractors.text: They have the same eigenvectors, since the eigenvalues coincide.
They have the same rank, since rank is the number of nonzero eigenvalues.
distractors.misconception: equates rank with the count of nonzero eigenvalues

distractors.text: They are similar if and only if they have the same trace and determinant.
They are similar as long as both matrices are invertible.
distractors.misconception: ignores the Jordan structure of repeated eigenvalues

explanation: The nilpotent matrix and $0$ both have characteristic polynomial $\lambda^2$ but different ranks, so they cannot be similar.

stem: How is the matrix $[T]_B^{B'}$ of $T:V\to W$ formed, for bases $B=(b_j)$ of $V$ and $B'$ of $W$?
correct: Its $j$th column is $[T(b_j)]_{B'}$, the image of the basis vector $b_j$ in the output basis.
Column $j$ holds the $B'$-coordinates of the image $T(b_j)$.

distractors.text: Its $j$th row is the coordinate vector $[T(b_j)]_{B'}$, written horizontally.
Its $j$th column is the $B$-coordinate vector of $b_j$ scaled by $T$.
distractors.misconception: mixes the domain basis and codomain basis

distractors.text: Its $j$th column is $T(e_j)$ in standard coordinates, whatever the bases.
Its $j$th column is the coordinate vector $[b_j]_{B'}$ of the basis vector itself.
Its $j$th column is the coordinate vector $[T(b_j)]_{B}$ in the domain basis instead.
distractors.misconception: expresses the image in the wrong basis

explanation: Column $j$ records how $T$ treats the $j$th input basis vector, expressed in the output basis. Then $[T(v)]_{B'}=[T]_B^{B'}[v]_B$.

stem: For a square matrix $A$, when is $\lambda$ an eigenvalue?
correct: Exactly when $\det(A-\lambda I)=0$, i.e. when the matrix $A-\lambda I$ is singular.
When $A-\lambda I$ has a nonzero kernel vector.

distractors.text: Exactly when $\det(A-\lambda I)=1$, i.e. when $A-\lambda I$ preserves volume.
distractors.misconception: confuses the zero determinant with volume preservation

distractors.text: Exactly when $A-\lambda I$ is invertible, so that $Av=\lambda v$ can be solved.
Exactly when $\lambda$ is a diagonal entry of $A$, for any matrix $A$.
Exactly when $\lambda$ divides $\det A$, a necessary divisibility condition.
Exactly when $\lambda\ne0$ and $A$ is invertible.

explanation: $Av=\lambda v$ with $v\ne0$ means $(A-\lambda I)v=0$ has a nontrivial solution, so $A-\lambda I$ is singular and its determinant vanishes.

stem: For an eigenvalue $\lambda$ of a matrix, which relation between the multiplicities always holds?
correct: $1\le\dim\ker(A-\lambda I)\le$ the algebraic multiplicity of $\lambda$.
Geometric multiplicity is at least $1$ and at most algebraic multiplicity.

distractors.text: The algebraic multiplicity is at most the geometric multiplicity.
The two multiplicities are always equal, for every square matrix.
The geometric multiplicity can exceed the algebraic multiplicity for special matrices.
The geometric multiplicity of a real eigenvalue is always exactly $1$.
The two multiplicities are equal exactly when $\lambda$ is a simple root.
distractors.misconception: confuses equality with simple roots; equality can also hold for repeated roots

explanation: The eigenspace has dimension at most the multiplicity of the root in the characteristic polynomial. For $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ the multiplicities are $2$ and $1$.

stem: Eigenvectors $v_1,\dots,v_k$ of a matrix belong to pairwise distinct eigenvalues. What follows?
correct: The vectors $v_1,\dots,v_k$ are linearly independent.
Eigenvectors for distinct eigenvalues cannot be linearly dependent.

distractors.text: The vectors are pairwise orthogonal, as in any matrix with distinct eigenvalues.
distractors.misconception: true only for symmetric or normal matrices

distractors.text: The vectors are linearly dependent once $k$ exceeds two.
distractors.misconception: believes independence breaks for many vectors

distractors.text: The vectors can be dependent, but then the eigenvalues must be zero.
distractors.misconception: invents a special role for the eigenvalue zero

distractors.text: The vectors form a basis of the whole space whenever $k\ge2$.
distractors.misconception: forgets that $k$ must equal the dimension

distractors.text: The vectors span a subspace on which the matrix acts as the identity.
distractors.misconception: confuses acting by $\lambda_i$ with acting trivially

explanation: Suppose a minimal dependence $\sum c_iv_i=0$; applying $A-\lambda_kI$ gives a shorter one. Orthogonality needs extra structure such as symmetry.

stem: Which statement about the eigenvalues of a square matrix $A$ is correct, counting algebraic multiplicity over $\mathbb{C}$?
correct: The trace is the sum of the eigenvalues and the determinant is their product.
$\operatorname{tr}A=\sum_i\lambda_i$ and $\det A=\prod_i\lambda_i$ with multiplicity.

distractors.text: The trace equals the sum of eigenvalues only if $A$ is diagonalizable.
The determinant equals the sum of the eigenvalues and the trace equals their product.
The trace is the sum of the real eigenvalues only, ignoring complex ones.
The determinant is the product of the nonzero eigenvalues only.
The identities hold for symmetric matrices but fail for triangular ones.
distractors.misconception: thinks they depend on matrix type

explanation: Both follow from the factorisation of the characteristic polynomial $\det(\lambda I-A)=\prod(\lambda-\lambda_i)$ by comparing coefficients, for every square matrix.

stem: Let $A$ be a real $3\times3$ matrix. Which statement is correct?
correct: $A$ has at least one real eigenvalue, since a real cubic has a real root.
Odd-size real matrices always have a real eigenvalue.

distractors.text: $A$ has three distinct real eigenvalues, since its characteristic polynomial has degree three.
distractors.misconception: confuses degree with the number of real roots

distractors.text: A non-real eigenvalue of $A$ can occur without its complex conjugate.
distractors.misconception: forgets conjugate pairs for real matrices

distractors.text: $A$ has no real eigenvalue whenever $\det A>0$.
distractors.misconception: links the sign of the determinant to realness

distractors.text: $A$ has a real eigenvalue only if $A$ is symmetric.
$A$ is diagonalizable over $\mathbb{C}$ whatever its entries.

explanation: Real polynomial roots occur in conjugate pairs and a cubic has three roots counted with multiplicity, so at least one is real. Even size fails: a rotation of the plane has none.

stem: When is an $n\times n$ matrix $A$ diagonalizable?
correct: Exactly when $A$ has $n$ linearly independent eigenvectors.
When there is a basis of eigenvectors.

distractors.text: Exactly when $A$ has $n$ distinct eigenvalues.
distractors.misconception: confuses a sufficient condition with a necessary one

distractors.text: Exactly when $A$ is invertible, so that no eigenvalue is zero.
Exactly when $A$ is symmetric, so that eigenvectors can be orthogonal.
Exactly when the characteristic polynomial has only real roots.
distractors.misconception: ignores the need for enough eigenvectors

distractors.text: Exactly when $\det A\ne0$ and $\operatorname{tr}A\ne0$.
distractors.misconception: invents a criterion from trace and determinant

explanation: $A=PDP^{-1}$ means the columns of $P$ are $n$ independent eigenvectors. Distinct eigenvalues suffice but are not necessary, and a real-rooted characteristic polynomial does not suffice.

stem: Why is $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ not diagonalizable?
correct: The eigenvalue $1$ has algebraic multiplicity $2$ but its eigenspace has dimension only $1$.
It has just one independent eigenvector, so no eigenbasis exists.

distractors.text: Because its determinant is $1$, and matrices with nonzero determinant are not diagonalizable.
Because it has a repeated eigenvalue, and repeated eigenvalues always prevent diagonalization.
Because it is not symmetric, and only symmetric matrices are diagonalizable.
Because its eigenvalue is not real, so the diagonal form cannot be written over $\mathbb{R}$.
Because its trace is $2$, and matrices with trace $2$ cannot be diagonalized.

explanation: $A-I=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ has rank $1$, so the eigenspace of $1$ is a line. A repeated eigenvalue prevents diagonalization only when the geometric multiplicity is smaller.

stem: If $A=PDP^{-1}$ with $D$ diagonal, which formula holds for $A^n$ with $n\ge1$?
correct: $A^n=PD^nP^{-1}$, where $D^n$ raises the diagonal entries to the $n$th power.
$A^n=PD^nP^{-1}$, with $D^n$ taken entrywise on the diagonal.

distractors.text: $A^n=P^nDP^{-n}$, as each factor is raised to the $n$th power.
distractors.misconception: powers the outer factors instead of the diagonal

distractors.text: $A^n=nPDP^{-1}$, as powers multiply a matrix by $n$.
$A^n=PDP^{-1}$ for all $n$, since conjugation does not change powers.
$A^n=D^nP^{-1}P$, because $P$ cancels against its inverse.
distractors.misconception: cancels factors in the wrong place

distractors.text: $A^n=P^{-1}D^nP$, with the roles of $P$ and $P^{-1}$ exchanged.

explanation: In $(PDP^{-1})^n$ the inner factors $P^{-1}P$ cancel, leaving $PD^nP^{-1}$.

stem: How are invertibility and diagonalizability of a square matrix related?
correct: Neither implies the other: $\operatorname{diag}(1,0)$ is singular yet diagonalizable, and a Jordan block is the reverse.
Neither property implies the other one.

distractors.text: Every invertible matrix is diagonalizable, since it has no zero eigenvalue.
Every diagonalizable matrix is invertible, since its diagonal form is well defined.
A singular matrix is never diagonalizable, as it has a nontrivial kernel.
distractors.misconception: forgets that the kernel is an eigenspace for zero

distractors.text: Diagonalizable matrices are exactly the invertible matrices with real eigenvalues.
An invertible matrix is diagonalizable if and only if its determinant is positive.

explanation: Diagonalizability concerns having enough eigenvectors; invertibility only concerns the eigenvalue $0$ not occurring.

stem: A matrix $A$ is diagonalizable. When does $A^n\to0$ as $n\to\infty$?
correct: When every eigenvalue satisfies $|\lambda|<1$.
Exactly when all eigenvalues lie inside the unit circle.

distractors.text: When at least one eigenvalue satisfies $|\lambda|<1$.
When every real eigenvalue satisfies $\lambda<1$, including large negative ones.
When $\det A<1$, since the volume shrinks to zero.
distractors.misconception: confuses the product of eigenvalues with each factor

distractors.text: When $\operatorname{tr}A<1$, since the diagonal entries stay small.
When $\det A=0$, so that some direction is collapsed to zero.
distractors.misconception: a single zero eigenvalue does not control the other directions

explanation: $A^n=PD^nP^{-1}$ and $D^n\to0$ exactly when every $|\lambda_i|<1$. A determinant below $1$ is not enough: $\operatorname{diag}(10,0.01)$ has $\det=0.1$ yet $A^n$ blows up.

stem: Two diagonalizable matrices $A$ and $B$ commute, $AB=BA$. What follows?
correct: They can be diagonalized by the very same invertible matrix.
They share a common basis of eigenvectors.

distractors.text: They must have the same eigenvalues, listed in the same order.
They must be equal up to a scalar multiple.
Their product is diagonalizable, but no common eigenbasis need exist.
One must be a polynomial in the other, as for any commuting pair.
distractors.misconception: confuses commuting with being polynomials of each other

distractors.text: They must have equal traces, since commuting matrices act alike.

explanation: Each eigenspace of $A$ is invariant under $B$, so $B$ can be diagonalized inside each one; together this gives a common eigenbasis. The converse also holds.

stem: Which property separates an inner product from a symmetric bilinear form that is only positive semidefinite?
correct: $\langle v,v\rangle=0$ implies $v=0$, positive definiteness.
Only the zero vector has self-pairing zero.

distractors.text: Symmetry: $\langle u,v\rangle=\langle v,u\rangle$ for all $u,v$.
distractors.misconception: both kinds of forms are symmetric

distractors.text: Linearity in the first argument for sums and scalars.
distractors.misconception: both kinds of forms are linear

distractors.text: Non-negativity: $\langle v,v\rangle\ge 0$ for every vector $v$.
Bounded values: $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le 1$ for all unit vectors.
Non-negativity of $\langle u,v\rangle$ for all pairs $u,v$.
distractors.misconception: inner products of different vectors can be negative

explanation: Semidefinite forms allow $\langle v,v\rangle=0$ for some $v\ne0$, which then has zero length. The definiteness axiom rules this out.

stem: When does equality $|\langle u,v\rangle|=\|u\|\|v\|$ hold in the Cauchy-Schwarz inequality?
correct: Exactly when $u$ and $v$ are linearly dependent vectors.
When one is a multiple of the other.

distractors.text: Exactly when $u$ and $v$ are orthogonal to each other.
Exactly when $\|u\|=\|v\|$, so the vectors have the same length.
Exactly when $u+v=0$, so the vectors are negatives of each other.
distractors.misconception: covers only one of the parallel cases

distractors.text: Exactly when $u$ and $v$ are linearly independent.
Exactly when the angle between $u$ and $v$ is $45^{\circ}$.

explanation: Equality means $\cos\theta=\pm1$, i.e. the vectors are parallel in the same or opposite sense. Orthogonal vectors give $\langle u,v\rangle=0$, the smallest left-hand side.

stem: On $\mathbb{R}^2$ define $\langle x,y\rangle=x_1y_1-x_2y_2$. Why is this not an inner product?
correct: Positive definiteness fails, e.g. $\langle(0,1),(0,1)\rangle=-1$.
Some nonzero $x$ has $\langle x,x\rangle<0$ here.

distractors.text: It is not symmetric in $x$ and $y$.
It is not linear in the first argument.
Because inner products must be positive for every pair of distinct vectors.
distractors.misconception: inner products of distinct vectors may be negative

distractors.text: Because an inner product space cannot contain orthogonal nonzero vectors.
distractors.misconception: orthogonal pairs are allowed in inner product spaces

distractors.text: It fails bilinearity in the second argument, since the sign is attached to one term.

explanation: Symmetry and bilinearity hold, but $\langle x,x\rangle=x_1^2-x_2^2$ is negative for $x=(0,1)$. A negative value alone for $\langle u,v\rangle$ is harmless.

stem: Which condition characterises the norms that come from an inner product?
correct: The parallelogram law $\|u+v\|^2+\|u-v\|^2=2\|u\|^2+2\|v\|^2$.
The parallelogram law holds for all pairs.

distractors.text: The triangle inequality $\|u+v\|\le\|u\|+\|v\|$ for all $u,v$.
The homogeneity rule $\|cv\|=|c|\|v\|$ for all scalars $c$.
The identity $\|u+v\|^2=\|u\|^2+\|v\|^2$ for all $u,v$.
Positivity: $\|v\|=0$ only for $v=0$ and $\|v\|\ge0$.
Completeness: every Cauchy sequence converges in the norm.
distractors.misconception: completeness is unrelated to inner products

explanation: Norms such as the max-norm on $\mathbb{R}^2$ satisfy the triangle inequality and homogeneity but not the parallelogram law, so they do not arise from an inner product.

stem: In a real inner product space, when does $\|u+v\|^2=\|u\|^2+\|v\|^2$ hold?
correct: Exactly when $u$ and $v$ are orthogonal vectors, i.e. $\langle u,v\rangle=0$.
Exactly when the cross term $\langle u,v\rangle$ vanishes.

distractors.text: Exactly when $u$ and $v$ are parallel vectors.
distractors.misconception: parallel vectors give the triangle equality, not Pythagoras

distractors.text: Exactly when $\|u\|=\|v\|$, so the vectors have equal length.
Exactly when both $u$ and $v$ are unit vectors.
Exactly when $u=-v$, so that the sum is zero.
Exactly when the angle between $u$ and $v$ is acute.
distractors.misconception: acute angles give a positive cross term

explanation: Expanding gives $\|u+v\|^2=\|u\|^2+2\langle u,v\rangle+\|v\|^2$, so equality holds exactly when the cross term $\langle u,v\rangle$ is zero.

stem: Why does $\cos\theta=\dfrac{\langle u,v\rangle}{\|u\|\|v\|}$ define a genuine angle in a real inner product space?
correct: The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality keeps the quotient in $[-1,1]$ for nonzero $u,v$.
The quotient never leaves $[-1,1]$ by Cauchy-Schwarz.

distractors.text: Because inner products of nonzero vectors are always positive, so $\theta$ is acute.
distractors.misconception: inner products can be negative or zero

distractors.text: Because $\|u\|\|v\|\le1$ for all vectors, so the quotient is small.
distractors.misconception: norms are not bounded by one

distractors.text: Because the triangle inequality bounds $\langle u,v\rangle$ by $\|u\|+\|v\|$.
Because the angle is defined only for orthogonal vectors, where it is $90^{\circ}$.
Because the formula is a definition and needs no justification at all.
distractors.misconception: ignores that arccos needs an argument in $[-1,1]$

explanation: The arccosine is defined on $[-1,1]$ only. The Cauchy-Schwarz inequality $|\langle u,v\rangle|\le\|u\|\|v\|$ guarantees the quotient lies there.

stem: In Gram-Schmidt, $w_k=v_k-\sum_{j<k}\langle v_k,e_j\rangle e_j$ with $e_1,\dots,e_{k-1}$ already orthonormal. What does this step achieve?
correct: It subtracts the components of $v_k$ along the earlier $e_j$ vectors.
$w_k$ is orthogonal to all earlier $e_j$ vectors.

distractors.text: It rescales $v_k$ to length $1$, so that $w_k$ is a unit vector.
It rotates $v_k$ into the plane spanned by $e_1$ and $e_2$.
It makes $w_k$ orthogonal to $v_k$ itself.
distractors.misconception: confuses the vector with the subspace

distractors.text: It replaces $v_k$ by an eigenvector of the Gram matrix.
It leaves the span of $v_1,\dots,v_k$ unchanged only if the $v_j$ are already orthogonal.

explanation: The sum is the orthogonal projection of $v_k$ onto $\operatorname{span}(e_1,\dots,e_{k-1})$; subtracting it leaves the part orthogonal to that span. The span of the first $k$ vectors is preserved.

stem: Let $W$ be a subspace of an inner product space $V$ and $v\in V$. Which condition characterises $p=P_Wv$?
correct: $p\in W$ and $v-p$ is orthogonal to every vector of $W$.
The unique $p\in W$ such that $v-p\perp W$ holds.

distractors.text: $p\in W$ and $v-p$ also lies in $W$.
$p\perp W$ and $v-p\in W$, so the roles are reversed.
distractors.misconception: swaps the subspace and its complement

distractors.text: $p$ is the unit vector in $W$ that points in the direction of $v$.
$p$ is the vector of $W$ with the largest inner product with $v$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the nearest vector with the largest inner product

distractors.text: $p=v$ whenever $v$ is orthogonal to $W$.

explanation: The projection is the unique $p\in W$ with $v-p\in W^{\perp}$, and it is also the nearest point of $W$ to $v$.

stem: For $A\in\mathbb{R}^{m\times n}$ and $b\in\mathbb{R}^m$, when is the least squares solution of $Ax\approx b$ unique?
correct: Exactly when the columns of $A$ are linearly independent.
When $A$ has full column rank, i.e. $A^{\top}A$ is invertible.

distractors.text: Exactly when $A$ is a square matrix.
Exactly when $b$ lies in the column space of $A$.
Exactly when $A$ has more rows than columns.
distractors.misconception: treats a necessary condition as sufficient

distractors.text: Exactly when $A^{\top}A=I$, so the columns are orthonormal.
Always, because the normal equations are always uniquely solvable.

explanation: The solutions of $A^{\top}Ax=A^{\top}b$ form a coset of $\ker(A^{\top}A)=\ker A$, a single point exactly when the columns are independent.

stem: Let $\hat x$ solve the least squares problem $\min\|Ax-b\|$. What can be said of the residual $r=b-A\hat x$?
correct: It is orthogonal to every column of $A$, that is $A^{\top}r=0$ holds.
$r$ is orthogonal to the column space of $A$.

distractors.text: It is zero, because least squares solves $Ax=b$ exactly.
distractors.misconception: confuses least squares with exact solving

distractors.text: It lies in the column space of $A$, along the fitted values.
distractors.misconception: confuses the residual with the fit

distractors.text: It is parallel to $\hat x$, so the error points along the solution.
It has the smallest possible entries, each one separately minimal.
distractors.misconception: confuses minimising the sum of squares with each entry

distractors.text: It is orthogonal to $b$, since the fit takes all of $b$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the residual with the fitted value

explanation: The normal equations $A^{\top}(b-A\hat x)=0$ say exactly that $r$ is orthogonal to the columns of $A$. The fit $A\hat x$ is the projection of $b$ onto the column space.

stem: Which pair of properties characterises a matrix $P$ of an orthogonal projection onto a subspace of $\mathbb{R}^n$?
correct: $P^2=P$ and $P^{\top}=P$ both hold.
$P$ is both idempotent and symmetric, as a matrix.

distractors.text: $P^2=P$ alone, with no further condition.
distractors.misconception: this gives all projections, including oblique ones

distractors.text: $P^{\top}P=I$, so that $P$ is an orthogonal matrix.
$P^2=2P$, since the projection doubles on the second application.
$P$ is invertible with eigenvalues between $0$ and $1$.
distractors.misconception: eigenvalues are exactly $0$ or $1$ and a projection onto a proper subspace is singular

distractors.text: $P^{\top}P=P^{\top}$ and $\det P=1$.
distractors.misconception: projections onto proper subspaces have zero determinant

explanation: Idempotence means projecting twice equals projecting once. Symmetry makes it orthogonal. The eigenvalues are $1$ on the subspace and $0$ on its complement.

stem: For a subspace $W$ of $\mathbb{R}^n$, which statement about $W^{\perp}$ is correct?
correct: $\dim W+\dim W^{\perp}=n$, and $(W^{\perp})^{\perp}=W$ holds.
Complement dimension is $n-\dim W$, and doing it twice gives $W$.

distractors.text: $\dim W^{\perp}=\dim W$ for every subspace $W$.
$W\cap W^{\perp}$ equals $W$, since each vector is orthogonal to itself.
$(W^{\perp})^{\perp}=W^{\perp}$, so taking the complement is idempotent.
distractors.misconception: confuses the complement with a projection

distractors.text: $W+W^{\perp}$ is a proper subspace unless $W=\{0\}$.
distractors.misconception: the sum is the whole space

distractors.text: $W^{\perp}$ always contains $W$, so every vector is orthogonal to its own subspace.

explanation: Write $\mathbb{R}^n=W\oplus W^{\perp}$. The intersection is $\{0\}$, the dimensions add to $n$, and applying the complement twice returns $W$ in finite dimensions.

stem: Let $T$ be an operator on a complex inner product space with orthonormal basis $B$ and $[T]_B=A$. What is $[T^*]_B$?
correct: The conjugate transpose $A^*=\bar A^{\top}$ of the matrix of $T$.
$\bar A^{\top}$, valid because $B$ is orthonormal.

distractors.text: The inverse $A^{-1}$, as $T^*$ undoes $T$.
The plain transpose $A^{\top}$, without conjugating the entries.
distractors.misconception: forgets the conjugation over complex fields

distractors.text: The adjugate (cofactor) matrix of $A$, since both are called adjoint.
distractors.misconception: confuses classical adjoint and operator adjoint

distractors.text: The matrix $\bar A^{\top}$ in any basis, orthonormal or not.
The matrix $A$ itself, since $\langle Tv,w\rangle=\langle v,Tw\rangle$.

explanation: The adjoint satisfies $\langle Tv,w\rangle=\langle v,T^*w\rangle$. In an orthonormal basis, this makes the matrix of $T^*$ the conjugate transpose.

stem: What do you know about the eigenvalues of a self-adjoint operator $T=T^*$?
correct: They are all real numbers.
Each eigenvalue is real, even over complex scalars.

distractors.text: They are all purely imaginary numbers.
They all have absolute value $1$.
They are all positive, since $T=T^*$ makes $\langle Tv,v\rangle>0$.
They can be non-real, but then come in conjugate pairs.
distractors.misconception: the conjugate pair rule applies to real non-symmetric matrices

distractors.text: They are real only when the space is finite dimensional.
distractors.misconception: the argument does not need dimension

explanation: If $Tv=\lambda v$ with $\|v\|=1$ then $\lambda=\langle Tv,v\rangle=\langle v,Tv\rangle=\bar\lambda$, so $\lambda$ is real.

stem: Which of these matrices is guaranteed to be normal, i.e. to satisfy $AA^*=A^*A$?
correct: Any unitary matrix $U$, since $UU^*=U^*U=I$.
Every matrix whose conjugate transpose equals its inverse.

distractors.text: Any invertible matrix, since $A$ has an inverse.
Any upper triangular matrix, since it has a simple form.
distractors.misconception: triangular matrices need not be normal

distractors.text: Any matrix with real entries, since transposition is then easy.
distractors.misconception: real matrices need not be normal

distractors.text: Any diagonalizable matrix, as its eigenvalues are visible.
distractors.misconception: diagonalizable matrices need not be normal

distractors.text: Any matrix with only positive entries.
distractors.misconception: positivity of entries gives no normality

explanation: Unitary, self-adjoint and skew-adjoint matrices are normal. Invertible, real, triangular or diagonalizable matrices need not be: $\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ is all four.

stem: Why is $A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$ not normal?
correct: $AA^{\top}=\begin{pmatrix}2&1\\1&1\end{pmatrix}$ differs from $A^{\top}A=\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&2\end{pmatrix}$.
$A$ does not commute with its own transpose.

distractors.text: Because $A$ is not symmetric, and normal matrices must be symmetric.
distractors.misconception: normal does not require symmetry, e.g. rotations

distractors.text: Because $A$ has a repeated eigenvalue, which normal matrices cannot have.
distractors.misconception: the identity is normal with repeated eigenvalue

distractors.text: Because $\det A=1\ne0$, whereas normal matrices are singular.
Because $A$ is not orthogonal, and normal matrices are orthogonal.
Because $A$ has a zero entry, and normal matrices have no zero entries.

explanation: Direct multiplication shows $AA^{\top}\ne A^{\top}A$. Rotations are normal without being symmetric, and the identity is normal with a repeated eigenvalue.

stem: Let $T$ be normal and $Tv=\lambda v$. What can be said about $T^*v$?
correct: $T^*v=\bar\lambda v$, so $v$ is also an eigenvector of $T^*$.
$v$ is an eigenvector of $T^*$ for $\bar\lambda$.

distractors.text: $T^*v=\lambda v$, with the same eigenvalue.
distractors.misconception: true only when the eigenvalue is real

distractors.text: $T^*v=-\lambda v$, the opposite eigenvalue.
$T^*v=\lambda^{-1}v$, the inverse eigenvalue.
$T^*v$ is orthogonal to $v$ for every eigenvector $v$.
$T^*v$ is not parallel to $v$ unless $T$ is self-adjoint.

explanation: For normal $T$, $\|(T-\lambda I)v\|=\|(T^*-\bar\lambda I)v\|$, so the eigenvector equation transfers to $T^*$ with $\bar\lambda$.

stem: For a real $n\times n$ matrix $A$, when is $A=Q\Lambda Q^{\top}$ possible with $Q$ orthogonal and $\Lambda$ diagonal?
correct: Exactly when $A$ is symmetric, that is $A=A^{\top}$ holds.
Iff $A$ equals its transpose.

distractors.text: Exactly when $A$ is normal, as in the complex spectral theorem.
distractors.misconception: rotations are normal but not real-orthogonally diagonalizable

distractors.text: Exactly when all eigenvalues of $A$ are real.
distractors.misconception: real eigenvalues do not exclude Jordan blocks

distractors.text: Exactly when $A$ is diagonalizable over $\mathbb{R}$.
Exactly when $A$ is invertible, so that $\Lambda$ has no zero entry.
distractors.misconception: confuses invertibility with the spectral theorem

distractors.text: Exactly when $A$ has $n$ distinct real eigenvalues.
distractors.misconception: sufficient for diagonalizability but not for orthogonality

explanation: The real spectral theorem is an equivalence: orthogonally diagonalizable real matrices are exactly symmetric ones. Normality is the right condition only over $\mathbb{C}$.

stem: Why is the rotation matrix $R_{\theta}$ of the plane, with $\theta\ne0,\pi$, not orthogonally diagonalizable over $\mathbb{R}$?
correct: Its eigenvalues $e^{\pm i\theta}$ are not real, but $Q\Lambda Q^{\top}$ has real ones.
It is not symmetric, and symmetry is required.

distractors.text: Because it is not a normal matrix, so no spectral theorem applies.
Because it is not an orthogonal matrix.
Because its eigenvectors over $\mathbb{C}$ are not orthogonal.
Because its determinant equals $-1$.
Because it has a repeated eigenvalue, so no basis of eigenvectors exists.
distractors.misconception: the eigenvalues are distinct over the complex numbers

explanation: Rotations are normal, so they are unitarily diagonalizable over $\mathbb{C}$ with eigenvalues $e^{\pm i\theta}$. Over $\mathbb{R}$ orthogonal diagonalizability requires symmetry.

stem: Let $A$ be real symmetric with eigenvectors $u$ and $w$ for different eigenvalues. What follows?
correct: $u$ and $w$ are orthogonal to each other.
Eigenvectors for different eigenvalues are perpendicular.

distractors.text: $u$ and $w$ are parallel, since they come from the same matrix.
$u$ and $w$ are orthogonal only after a Gram-Schmidt step.
distractors.misconception: orthogonality is automatic across different eigenvalues

distractors.text: $u$ and $w$ are orthogonal for every real matrix with distinct eigenvalues.
$u$ and $w$ are orthogonal only if both eigenvalues are positive.
$u$ and $w$ have equal length, since both come from the same matrix.

explanation: $\lambda\langle u,w\rangle=\langle Au,w\rangle=\langle u,Aw\rangle=\mu\langle u,w\rangle$ gives $(\lambda-\mu)\langle u,w\rangle=0$, so $\langle u,w\rangle=0$.

stem: Let $A=\sum_i\lambda_iu_iu_i^{\top}$ be the spectral decomposition of a real symmetric matrix with orthonormal $u_i$. What is each $u_iu_i^{\top}$?
correct: The orthogonal projection onto the line $\mathbb{R}u_i$.
A rank-one symmetric projection.

distractors.text: The identity matrix restricted to $\mathbb{R}u_i$, of rank $n$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the projection with the identity

distractors.text: An orthogonal matrix whose columns are the $u_i$.
distractors.misconception: confuses outer product with the matrix $Q$

distractors.text: A diagonal matrix with $\lambda_i$ in position $i$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the projection with the diagonal factor

distractors.text: The inverse of $\lambda_iu_iu_i^{\top}$.
A matrix of rank $n-1$ that kills $u_i$ and fixes its orthogonal complement.
distractors.misconception: describes the projection onto the complement

explanation: $(u_iu_i^{\top})^2=u_iu_i^{\top}$ and it is symmetric of rank one, hence the projection onto $\mathbb{R}u_i$. The $u_iu_i^{\top}$ sum to the identity.

stem: Two real symmetric matrices $A$ and $B$. When do they share an orthonormal basis of eigenvectors?
correct: Exactly when they commute, that is $AB=BA$ holds.
They do exactly when $AB=BA$.

distractors.text: Always, because both have orthonormal eigenbases.
distractors.misconception: each has its own basis but they need not agree

distractors.text: Exactly when they have the same eigenvalues.
distractors.misconception: confuses common eigenvectors with equal spectra

distractors.text: Exactly when $A+B$ is symmetric, which is automatic.
distractors.misconception: the sum is always symmetric, so this is no condition

distractors.text: Exactly when $AB$ is symmetric and invertible.
Exactly when $A$ and $B$ have the same rank.
distractors.misconception: rank is unrelated to a common eigenbasis

explanation: Commuting symmetric matrices are simultaneously orthogonally diagonalizable, and conversely diagonal matrices commute. Symmetry of $AB$ is equivalent to commuting, but invertibility is irrelevant.

stem: For a real symmetric matrix $A$, which test shows that $A$ is positive definite?
correct: All eigenvalues of the matrix $A$ are strictly positive.
Leading minors all positive.

distractors.text: All diagonal entries of $A$ are positive.
The determinant of $A$ is positive.
distractors.misconception: an even number of negative eigenvalues also gives positive determinant

distractors.text: All entries of $A$ are positive.
The trace of $A$ is positive.
distractors.misconception: one large eigenvalue can hide negative ones

distractors.text: The inequality $x^{\top}Ax\ge0$ holds for all vectors $x$.
distractors.misconception: that is semidefiniteness, which allows zero values

explanation: Both criteria are equivalent for symmetric matrices. $\begin{pmatrix}1&2\\2&1\end{pmatrix}$ has positive diagonal and entries but eigenvalues $3$ and $-1$.

stem: Which test is valid for positive semidefiniteness of a real symmetric matrix?
correct: Every principal minor is nonnegative.
Each principal minor is $\ge0$.

distractors.text: All leading principal minors are nonnegative.
The determinant is nonnegative.
distractors.misconception: $-I$ has positive determinant in even size

distractors.text: All diagonal entries are nonnegative.
The trace is nonnegative.
distractors.misconception: one large eigenvalue hides negative ones

distractors.text: At least one eigenvalue is nonnegative.

explanation: For semidefiniteness leading minors do not suffice. For $\operatorname{diag}(0,-1)$ the leading minors are $0,0$, yet the form is negative on $e_2$.

stem: A $2\times2$ real symmetric matrix has one positive and one negative eigenvalue. What is the curve $x^{\top}Ax=1$?
correct: A hyperbola, never an ellipse or circle.
A hyperbola, because the form is indefinite.

distractors.text: An ellipse, because the equation is quadratic.
A circle, since the equation has a constant right side.
A parabola, since there is a sign change.
distractors.misconception: parabolas arise from degenerate forms with a linear term

distractors.text: The empty set, since the form can be negative.
distractors.misconception: the form also takes positive values

distractors.text: A pair of intersecting lines, since the form factorises.
distractors.misconception: factorisation happens only when the right side is zero

explanation: In principal axes the equation is $\lambda_1y_1^2+\lambda_2y_2^2=1$ with $\lambda_1>0>\lambda_2$, a hyperbola.

stem: A covariance matrix $\Sigma$ of a random vector $X$ is always which kind of matrix?
correct: Symmetric positive semidefinite, since $a^{\top}\Sigma a=\operatorname{Var}(a^{\top}X)\ge0$.
Symmetric with nonnegative eigenvalues.

distractors.text: Positive definite, whatever the random vector.
distractors.misconception: perfectly dependent variables give zero eigenvalues

distractors.text: Entrywise nonnegative, since variances are nonnegative.
Diagonal, since variables are always taken as uncorrelated.
Orthogonal, with determinant equal to $1$.
Symmetric with all eigenvalues at most $1$, since covariances are bounded by one.

explanation: The quadratic form is a variance and so is nonnegative. It is strictly positive for all $a\ne0$ only if no nontrivial combination of the components is constant.

stem: When is a covariance matrix $\Sigma$ singular?
correct: Some nonzero combination has zero variance.
When some $a^{\top}X$ is constant.

distractors.text: When the variables are uncorrelated.
distractors.misconception: uncorrelated variables with positive variance give a positive definite diagonal matrix

distractors.text: When all correlations are positive.
distractors.misconception: positive correlations can still be non-singular

distractors.text: When the variables are independent.
distractors.misconception: independent non-degenerate variables give a diagonal positive definite matrix

distractors.text: When some variable has variance $1$.
distractors.misconception: the scale of one variance does not matter

distractors.text: When the covariance matrix has negative entries.
distractors.misconception: negative entries do not imply singularity

explanation: $\Sigma a=0$ for $a\ne0$ means $a^{\top}\Sigma a=\operatorname{Var}(a^{\top}X)=0$, so $a^{\top}X$ is constant: an exact linear dependence among the variables.

stem: For a real symmetric matrix $A$, what is $\max_{\|x\|=1}x^{\top}Ax$?
correct: The largest eigenvalue of the matrix $A$.
The top eigenvalue, $\lambda_{\max}(A)$.

distractors.text: The largest absolute value of an eigenvalue.
distractors.misconception: differs when the most extreme eigenvalue is negative

distractors.text: The sum of all eigenvalues, i.e. the trace.
The largest diagonal entry of $A$.
distractors.misconception: diagonal entries are only lower bounds on $\lambda_{\max}$

distractors.text: The determinant of $A$.
distractors.misconception: confuses the maximum with a product

distractors.text: The smallest eigenvalue of $A$.
distractors.misconception: gives the minimum rather than the maximum

explanation: Writing $x=Qy$ gives $\sum\lambda_iy_i^2$ with $\sum y_i^2=1$, maximised by putting all weight on the largest eigenvalue. With eigenvalues $-5,1$ the maximum is $1$, not $5$.

stem: Under a congruence $A\mapsto P^{\top}AP$ with $P$ invertible, what stays the same for symmetric $A$?
correct: Eigenvalue sign counts (the inertia).
The signature of the form.

distractors.text: The eigenvalues themselves.
The determinant of the matrix.
distractors.misconception: only the sign of the determinant is preserved

distractors.text: The trace of the matrix.
The eigenvectors as vectors in $\mathbb{R}^n$.
The condition number of $A$.
distractors.misconception: the condition number changes under congruence

explanation: Congruence changes coordinates of the form $x^{\top}Ax$, so definiteness persists while the eigenvalues, trace and determinant magnitude change. For example $P=2I$ scales $A$ by $4$.

stem: How are the singular values of a real matrix $A$ defined?
correct: They are the square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^{\top}A$.
The square roots of eigenvalues of $A^{\top}A$.

distractors.text: They are the eigenvalues of $A^{\top}A$ themselves.
They are the absolute values of the eigenvalues of $A$ for every square matrix.
They are the diagonal entries of $A$ after row reduction.
They are the lengths of the rows of $A$.
distractors.misconception: confuses row norms with singular values

distractors.text: They are the square roots of the eigenvalues of $A^2$.

explanation: $A^{\top}A$ is positive semidefinite, so its eigenvalues $\sigma_i^2$ are nonnegative. For $\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\0&0\end{pmatrix}$ the eigenvalues of $A$ are $0,0$ but $\sigma_1=1$.

stem: How does the rank of a real matrix show up in its singular values?
correct: The rank equals the number of nonzero singular values of the matrix.
Rank counts the positive singular values.

distractors.text: The rank equals the number of nonzero eigenvalues of $A$.
distractors.misconception: nilpotent matrices have rank above their eigenvalue count

distractors.text: The rank equals the number of distinct singular values.
The rank equals the number of singular values larger than $1$.
The rank equals the largest singular value rounded up.
The rank equals the number of singular values equal to the largest one.
distractors.misconception: counts only the top singular value

explanation: In $A=U\Sigma V^{\top}$ the rank of $A$ is the rank of $\Sigma$, the number of positive diagonal entries.

stem: What does the Eckart-Young theorem say about the best rank-$k$ approximation of $A$?
correct: The truncated SVD $A_k=\sum_{i\le k}\sigma_iu_iv_i^{\top}$ minimises the error in both norms.
Keeping the $k$ largest singular triples is optimal.

distractors.text: Keeping the $k$ largest entries of $A$ and zeroing the rest is optimal.
Keeping the $k$ rows of $A$ with the largest norms is optimal.
The eigendecomposition truncated to $k$ terms is optimal for every square matrix.
Zeroing the $k$ largest singular values gives the optimal approximation.
distractors.misconception: keeps the smallest instead of the largest

distractors.text: Rounding every entry of $A$ to $k$ decimal places is optimal.

explanation: The error is $\|A-A_k\|_2=\sigma_{k+1}$ and $\|A-A_k\|_F^2=\sum_{i>k}\sigma_i^2$, and no rank-$k$ matrix does better.

stem: How are the principal component directions of a data matrix $X$ obtained?
correct: They are the right singular vectors of the column-centred matrix $X$.
Top eigenvectors of the covariance matrix.

distractors.text: They are the left singular vectors of the centred matrix $X$.
distractors.misconception: left vectors live in observation space

distractors.text: They are the right singular vectors of $X$ computed without centring the columns.
distractors.misconception: centring is part of the definition

distractors.text: They are the eigenvectors with the smallest eigenvalues of the covariance.
They are the coordinate axes along the variables with the largest variance.
They are the rows of $X$ with the largest norms.

explanation: With $X$ centred, the sample covariance is $X^{\top}X/(n-1)=V\Sigma^2V^{\top}/(n-1)$, so the columns of $V$ are the principal directions and the variances are $\sigma_i^2/(n-1)$.

stem: What fraction of the total variance does the $i$th principal component explain?
correct: The share $\lambda_i/\sum_j\lambda_j$ of covariance eigenvalues in the total variance.
$\sigma_i^2$ divided by the sum of all squared singular values.

distractors.text: The ratio $\sigma_i/\sum_j\sigma_j$ of the unsquared singular values.
distractors.misconception: variance scales like the square of a singular value

distractors.text: The eigenvalue $\lambda_i$ divided by the number of observations $n$.
distractors.misconception: forgets to divide by the total variance

distractors.text: The proportion $1/p$ of the $p$ variables, whatever the data.
The ratio of the $i$th diagonal entry of the covariance to its trace.
distractors.misconception: this is the share of a single variable

distractors.text: The partial sum $\lambda_1+\dots+\lambda_i$ divided by the number $p$ of variables.
distractors.misconception: confuses a cumulative sum with a share

explanation: Variance along a principal direction is $\lambda_i=\sigma_i^2/(n-1)$, and the total variance is $\operatorname{tr}\Sigma=\sum_j\lambda_j$.

stem: Which statement about the SVD is correct?
correct: Every real $m\times n$ matrix has an SVD $A=U\Sigma V^{\top}$ of any rank.
An SVD exists for every real matrix.

distractors.text: It exists only for square matrices, as with eigendecomposition.
It exists only for invertible matrices.
distractors.misconception: rank deficient matrices have an SVD

distractors.text: It exists only for symmetric matrices.
distractors.misconception: this is the condition for orthogonal diagonalization

distractors.text: It exists only if $A$ has real eigenvalues.
It exists only for matrices with full column rank.
distractors.misconception: rank deficiency just gives zero singular values

explanation: $A^{\top}A$ is symmetric positive semidefinite, hence orthogonally diagonalizable; this gives $V$ and $\Sigma$, and $U$ follows from $Av_i=\sigma_iu_i$.

stem: Let $Z=XV$ be the principal component scores of a centred data matrix $X$. What holds for them?
correct: Their covariance matrix is diagonal, with the variances $\lambda_i$ on its diagonal.
The scores are uncorrelated with each other.

distractors.text: Their sample covariance is the identity matrix.
distractors.misconception: whitening requires dividing by the standard deviations

distractors.text: They are statistically independent, whatever the distribution of the data.
Their variances are all equal.
Their correlations equal the correlations of the original variables.
distractors.misconception: rotation to scores removes the correlations

distractors.text: Their sample covariance matrix equals that of $X$, as $V$ is orthogonal.
distractors.misconception: an orthogonal change of axes removes the correlations

explanation: $Z^{\top}Z/(n-1)=V^{\top}(X^{\top}X/(n-1))V=\Lambda$. Independence would need extra assumptions such as joint normality.
